lesson.title: Adjektive: richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen
lesson.subtitle: five adjectives English kept almost intact — and the proof that German is English in other sounds

hook.title: Right, False, Open — and the Closing Proof
hook.content: The last new words of the campaign, and they prove the method one final time. richtig is right — one Proto-Germanic word, *rehtaz, that both languages kept: English right, German recht, and richtig is recht with the adjective tail -ig, 'right-ish' turned exact. The gh in right and the ch-sound in recht are the same ancient letter — the family that made light/Licht and night/Nacht — and das Recht, 'the right, the law', lives in the idiom Du hast recht, 'you are right'. falsch is the borrowed one: Latin falsus, 'deceived, false' — German took it straight from Latin, English took it through Old French as false; same word, two routes, one meaning. offen and open are the same ancient word — and the shift is right there in its middle: German's great P→PF law turned pipe into Pfeife, and it did the same quiet work here, turning open's p into offen's ff, exactly as it did in pepper/Pfeffer and apple/Apfel. Same word, one shift, and you can hear it every morning. sauber and leer are the honest limitations: no safe English twin has been proven for either — clean and empty are places where English and German walked apart. Sisters share most of their words; they do not share all of them. That is the whole method in five adjectives: two twins, one double purchase, one twin with the shift working in its middle, and two words with no twin at all.

footnotes.title: The Shift, Working in the Middle
footnotes.content: The P→PF law filled German with pf-words — Pfeife (pipe), Pfeffer (pepper), Pfund (pound) — and offen is one of its successes, not one of its exceptions. Open and offen are the same ancient word, and the law did its quiet work in the middle: English p became German ff, the same shift you can see in apple/Apfel and hear in pepper/Pfeffer. No exception to file away — this one you can hold in your hand every morning precisely because the shift kept the word recognizable.

pattern.title: The Adjective After sein
pattern.content: 1. Predicate position, no ending: Das Glas ist leer, Das Fenster ist offen, Die Klingel ist richtig laut. 2. The judging pair: Die Zahl ist richtig, die Zahl ist falsch — richtig approves, falsch rejects. The fixed idiom: Du hast recht — 'you are right' — uses das Recht, the older noun. 3. richtig doubles as an intensifier: Der Kellner ist richtig nett — 'really nice'. 4. Everything can be sauber or leer: Seife macht sauber; Nach dem Frühstück ist der Herd sauber; der Keller ist leer. 5. Colors fit the same frame: Die Farbe der Mütze ist lila.
pattern.linguist_note: This is the last lesson with new words, and it closes on the campaign's oldest truth: most of German is already English wearing different sounds. richtig/right, falsch/false and offen/open are single words in two costumes; even falsch, the foreign-looking one, is the same Latin falsus both languages bought. What remains is raw material — a language you can now read through its shifts, its loans and its twins. The whole compendium waits in review, and every review is a reunion.

exercises.prompt: The house, judged — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The mirror and the rug are clean
matching_pairs.german: Der Spiegel und der Teppich sind sauber

matching_pairs.english: The door to the balcony is open
matching_pairs.german: Die Tür zum Balkon ist offen

matching_pairs.english: After breakfast the stove is clean
matching_pairs.german: Nach dem Frühstück ist der Herd sauber

matching_pairs.english: The guest leaves, the house is empty
matching_pairs.german: Der Gast geht, das Haus ist leer

matching_pairs.english: We are right, the school is empty
matching_pairs.german: Wir sind richtig, die Schule ist leer

exercises.target_answer: Der Flur ist sauber, Der Spiegel und der Teppich sind sauber, Der Schrank ist offen, Die Tür zum Balkon ist offen, Nach dem Frühstück ist der Herd sauber, Seife macht sauber, Zucker im Tee? Falsch!, Der Gast geht, das Haus ist leer, Die Gruppe zählt richtig, Der Held ist nie falsch, Wir sind richtig, die Schule ist leer, Sauber wie beim Friseur
exercises.meaning: clean, empty, open, right, wrong — the house, judged
exercises.explanation: Five adjectives, the whole house. sauber does the chores — der Flur, der Spiegel, der Herd — while leer and offen move through the rooms. And the course's people get judged one last time: die Gruppe zählt richtig, der Held ist nie falsch.

exercises.prompt: One of today's five is a Latin loan that English also bought. Which?
exercises.meaning: falsch ← Latin falsus → false: the double purchase
exercises.explanation: richtig and offen are inherited twins; sauber and leer have no proven twin. falsch is the purchase: Latin falsus, taken directly into German and through Old French into English as false.

exercises.prompt: 'richtig' is recht + -ig — and recht is the same ancient word as its English twin, the gh and ch being one letter. Give the English twin:
exercises.explanation: right and recht are one word — the same family as light/Licht and night/Nacht. English spelled the old sound gh and went silent; German kept ch. richtig adds the -ig tail: right-ish, made exact.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the basement verdict: 'The cellar is empty'
exercises.explanation: der Keller, masculine, from the Wohnen lessons. The other tiles are the lesson's other verdicts — the frame never changes: der/die/das + ist + adjective.
exercises.affirmation: The frame is five words long and judges a whole house.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the waiter's review: 'The waiter is really nice'
exercises.explanation: richtig does double duty: it judges (die Zahl ist richtig) and it intensifies (richtig nett, richtig laut). The sentence borrows the Kellner from the Berufe lessons and the nett from the last one.

summary.outcome: Judge and describe with richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen — and close the campaign on its oldest proof.

use_example.german: Der Gast geht, das Haus ist leer — die Tür zum Balkon ist offen.
use_example.english: The guest leaves, the house is empty — the door to the balcony is open.

summary.takeaway: richtig is right with the gh↔ch badge, falsch is Latin falsus bought twice, offen is open with the shift working in its middle (p became ff, as in Apfel) — and sauber and leer have no twins: even sisters have words the other never had.
summary.curiosity_teaser: This campaign ends here — the shifts, the twins, the borrowed shelves: the whole compendium waits in review.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Adjektive: richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen (The waiter is really nice):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Der Kellner ist richtig nett" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Adjektive: richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen without relying on short-term echo.

richtig.etymology_derivation: recht (right, the gh→ch twin) + -ig — 'right-y', the same root as English right. [wiktionary]

falsch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *falskī, from Latin falsus — the same Latin line as English false. [wiktionary]

sauber.etymology_derivation: Ultimately from Latin sobrius — the same Latin word behind English sober. [wiktionary]

leer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lēziz — English leer is the listed cognate, both originally 'empty'. [wiktionary]

offen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *opan — English open is listed among cognates, kin to auf. [wiktionary]

schwarz.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *swartaz — the true English twin is swart/swarthy; English black is a different Germanic word. [wiktionary]

keller.context_translation: The bicycles are standing in the basement.
keller.etymology_derivation: From Old High German kellari, from West Germanic kellari, an early loan of Late Latin cellarium; English cellar is the same Latin word through Old French. [wiktionary]

flur.context_translation: The shoes are standing in the hallway.
flur.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic floraz; English floor is a direct cognate that kept the old sense, while German Flur narrowed to mean hallway. [wiktionary]

teppich.context_phrase: Der Teppich liegt unter dem Tisch.
teppich.context_translation: The rug is under the table.
teppich.etymology_derivation: Via Medieval Latin tapicus, from Latin tapes; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

schrank.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skrankaz 'grid, barrier'; no English cognate — memorize this one (see der Kühlschrank). [wiktionary]

spiegel.context_phrase: Der Spiegel hängt an der Wand.
spiegel.context_translation: The mirror hangs on the wall.
spiegel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *spēgl, an early adoption of Latin speculum; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

vorhang.etymology_derivation: vor (in front) + hängen (hang) — 'the front-hang'; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

balkon.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French balcon, Italian balcone — a Romance loan; no Germanic root. [wiktionary]

herd.context_phrase: Der Topf steht auf dem Herd.
herd.context_translation: The pot is on the stove.
herd.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic herth; English hearth is a direct cognate, the English th corresponding to German d. [wiktionary]

seife.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic saipo, from the PIE root seyb, meaning to pour or trickle; English soap is a direct cognate, its p corresponding to German f after the High German shift. [wiktionary]

kamm.context_phrase: Ich brauche einen Kamm für die Haare.
kamm.context_translation: I need a comb for my hair.
kamm.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kambaz, from PIE gombhos, meaning tooth; English comb is a direct cognate, and both keep the old idea that a comb is full of teeth. [wiktionary]

klingel.context_phrase: Die Klingel läutet an der Tür.
klingel.context_translation: The doorbell is ringing at the door.
klingel.etymology_derivation: From the verb klingen, meaning to ring or sound; the same Germanic kling root underlies English clink. [wiktionary]

zucker.context_phrase: Ich nehme Zucker in den Kaffee.
zucker.context_translation: I take sugar in my coffee.
zucker.etymology_derivation: Via Italian zucchero from Arabic sukkar, Sanskrit śárkarā — the same trade-route loan as English sugar. [wiktionary]

gast.context_phrase: Wir haben heute Gäste zum Essen.
gast.context_translation: We have guests for dinner today.
gast.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *gastiz, the exact twin of English guest; Latin hostis, enemy, shows the older guest-host pair. [wiktionary]

gruppe.context_phrase: Unsere Gruppe trifft sich um acht.
gruppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, ultimately from Germanic *kruppaz, lump — the same Romance round-trip word as English group. [wiktionary]

held.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, hero, cognate with Old English hæleþ, a relative of the English health and hale family; the final th hardened to d. [wiktionary]

arbeiter.context_phrase: Der Arbeiter kommt um sieben Uhr.
arbeiter.context_translation: The worker comes at seven o'clock.
arbeiter.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of arbeiten (work) + -er; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

kellner.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin cellenarius (cellarer), from Late Latin cellarium - the pantry word that also gave German Keller and English cellar. [wiktionary][etymonline]

lila.etymology_derivation: From French lilas — a French loan in German; English lilac comes from the same French/Arabic source. [wiktionary]

wir.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīz — the very same pronoun as English we. [wiktionary]

schule.context_phrase: Die Schule beginnt um acht Uhr.
schule.etymology_derivation: From Latin (ultimately Greek scholē) — the same classical loan as English school; see Schüler. [wiktionary]

friseur.etymology_derivation: A French-style formation from frisieren; no standard English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

farbe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *farwō 'color' (Old High German farawa), from the PIE root *perḱ- 'colored'; no English cognate is listed on the page. [wiktionary]

segel.context_phrase: Das weiße Segel weht im Wind.
segel.context_translation: The white sail blows in the wind.

nachts.context_phrase: Nachts ist es hier ganz still.
nachts.context_translation: At night it is completely quiet here.
nachts.etymology_derivation: Nacht + adverbial -s — the entry lists the English adverb nights as a cognate; Nacht is night with gh → ch. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
